Founder, Brand and Community Accounts Need Different Jobs

By lowob · August 7, 2026 · Updated 10 November 2026 · 4-minute read · Growth / Social

When a founder, company and community account all repeat the same announcement, people have fewer reasons to follow each one. Give every account a distinct purpose.

Many startups operate several social accounts but only one voice.

The founder posts corporate announcements. The company account tries to sound personal. Community channels repeat the same copy with more emojis. Every surface distributes the same message without adding context, credibility, or participation.

This wastes the reason those channels exist separately.

A founder, a company, and a community have different sources of authority. A useful social system assigns each one a distinct job.

The founder account: judgment and conviction

People follow founders to understand how they see the world, why they are building, and how they make decisions.

That can mean explaining a difficult tradeoff, sharing a lesson from building, recognizing a customer or partner, or expressing a view on where the market is heading. The founder has credibility because they are close to these decisions, not because they repeat the latest press release.

It should not become a copy-and-paste distribution endpoint for every press release. A founder's credibility comes from proximity to the decisions and willingness to express a real view.

The company account: clarity and proof

The company account is the canonical source for what the organization knows, offers, ships, and can substantiate.

Use it for reliable product explanations, launches, customer and partner evidence, helpful educational resources, event information, recruiting updates and corrections. Readers should know where to find the authoritative version of a claim.

Its tone can be recognizable without pretending to be a person. The standard is clarity, consistency, and reliability.

Community channels: participation and interpretation

Community surfaces should help members understand, discuss, question, and extend what the company is doing.

Member questions, feedback, working sessions and resources created by the community belong here. Members should be able to contribute knowledge and interpret product news for one another, rather than waiting for staff to supply every conversation.

The company may facilitate the environment, but community value should increasingly move between members.

Use a message cascade

One important announcement can appear across all three surfaces without becoming identical.

Suppose a company launches a new institutional product.

Founder: Explains why the product had to exist, what the team learned from early buyers, and what belief drove the decision.

Company: Publishes the authoritative explanation, functionality, eligibility, proof, and next steps.

Community: Hosts a question session, gathers implementation feedback, surfaces member use cases, and preserves answers.

The underlying fact is consistent. The value added by each voice is different.

Define boundaries before a difficult moment

Account roles become especially important during incidents, rumors, market volatility, or criticism.

Decide which account publishes confirmed facts, when a founder speaks personally, what moderators can answer and when legal, security or executive review is required. Keep updates in one durable place so speculation cannot replace the company's official account.

Without these rules, urgency produces contradictory messages and unauthorized interpretation.

Create a practical operating matrix

Give each recurring content type a primary account, a responsible owner, any required approval and a way to measure success. Supporting accounts should add context or participation, not copy the original announcement.

A market opinion may belong primarily to the founder and be measured through qualified discussion. A product launch belongs to the company and is measured through comprehension and action. A contributor program belongs to community operations and is measured through participation and output.

Do not force equal activity

The three account types do not need identical publishing frequencies.

A founder may post only when they have something worth saying. The company may maintain a predictable editorial cadence. Community channels may be active every day because members are interacting. Consistency means fulfilling the account's promise, not hitting the same quota everywhere.

Resource-constrained teams should begin with the surfaces that match their actual objectives. A founder selling enterprise software may benefit more from a strong personal LinkedIn presence and company knowledge base than from maintaining six weak channels. A consumer crypto network may require much stronger real-time community operations.

Social strategy becomes simpler when each account answers one question:

Why should someone follow this source in addition to the others?

If the answer is unclear, the account does not yet have a job.

Selected source: a16z crypto: Social media for startups

lowob takeaways

  • Give each account a useful audience and specific job.
  • Keep the facts consistent while varying how they're explained.
  • Coordinate a shared brief instead of publishing identical posts.
